doc.title: Ray Blue interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 23, 2022

title: Mentally slowing down fast changes
summary: Blue describes slowing down fast tunes mentally so phrases fall in place.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If you’re playing an uptempo standard that has a significant number of changes and they’re going by fairly quickly, is it possible to tell us what is going on in your head as you’re playing?

Yeah. Slow it down. I want to slow it down. For me. I’ll slow it down. Because you don’t want to approach it in a frantic way. So in your head you’re slowing it down. Now the changes are moving and the changes are moving along, well you look at the changes, you check out the changes and see how they connect you know, and where they connect. You know some are passing, some need to be pronounced, and hear how the rhythm is working and the time. And then so when you speak your phrases they’ll fall in place, they’ll fall in place. That’s how I put it. I slow it down. Like you’ve got something that’s moving really fast and then you want to kind of subdivide you know, you want to slow it down a little so that you hear and see everything you know. You’re going to hear, your ears tell you a lot, your ears tell you a lot, and then what you’ve been practicing, studying, you know some stuff. You don’t rely totally on your ears but you’ve got to know stuff. But what I do — my way of doing it is I’ll slow it down and then even though the time didn’t stop, doesn’t slow down, I’ll slow it down mentally so I can speak to what I’m hearing. Yeah. That’s how I do it.
Nice way to put it. And you said you’ve got to know some stuff.
